faqs.q: Rats and raccoons are in our Ocala barn — where do we start?
faqs.a: With the feed, as always: sweet feed in open bags is a raccoon and rat cafeteria. Metal cans with locking lids, a swept feed room, and cats' food brought in at night collapse most of the draw. Then we trap the residents, seal the barn's eave and door gaps with hardware cloth, and check the hay storage for nesting. Barns that stay open at the eaves refill; barns that close, with feed secured, stay quiet through the season — that sequence is the whole program, and we quote it as one job.

Ocala.wildlife_intro:
Ocala is Horse Capital country — thoroughbred farms behind white fences, a historic downtown, and suburbs spreading through oak hammock and former pasture in every direction. The horse landscape defines the wildlife work: raccoons and rats in barns and feed rooms rival attic calls, gray squirrels own the canopy neighborhoods, armadillos dig the pastures and lawns, and the Ocala National Forest at the county's east sends the full forest cast to its edge communities. Downtown's older buildings hold bat colonies each summer.

Farm-first service is our Ocala pattern: the inspection covers house and barn together, feed storage gets hardened, and the plan ranks animal-proofing by what protects horses and feed. In town, canopy squirrel work and chimney raccoons lead. Forest-edge subdivisions get tortoise literacy and bear-aware trash advice — Marion County has real bear country east, and FWC's program, not a trapper, owns that file.

faqs.q: Skunks keep denning under our Dunnellon cottage — how is that fixed for good?
faqs.a: Evict, confirm, skirt. We trap or one-way-door the skunks at their dug entry, verify the crawl space is empty, then skirt the cottage with screening set into a buried apron so digging under fails. Dunnellon's sandy soil makes the buried apron non-negotiable — surface skirting in sand is a suggestion, not a barrier. Keep the yard's pet food in and the woodpile off the ground, and the cottage stays skunk-free in a town where skunks are simply part of the fauna.

faqs.q: What is digging in my Belleview yard — the holes are everywhere?
faqs.a: Count the shapes. Many small cone-shaped holes scattered widely mean an armadillo feeding at night. A system of raised tunnels means an eastern mole. One large half-moon burrow with a sand apron means a gopher tortoise — protected, and the digging stops being a service question and becomes a buffer-and-referral answer. Belleview's sandy ground hosts all three, often on the same street; the inspection sorts yours before a dollar of treatment is quoted.

faqs.q: We bought a lot in the Shores with a big burrow — what is it?
faqs.a: On this dry sandy ground, a wide half-moon burrow with a pale sand apron is a gopher tortoise until proven otherwise — State Threatened, protected, and requiring an FWC permit and an Authorized Agent for any relocation tied to building. An armadillo burrow is smaller, rounder, and tucked against cover. Bring us in before design money is spent: we identify the burrow, mark the 25-foot buffer if it is a tortoise's, and you plan with the fact instead of discovering it at permitting.

faqs.q: Why do new Marion Oaks homes get roof rats so fast?
faqs.a: Because construction concentrates them. Clearing and building displace the rats living in the surrounding lots, and a fresh house offers warm attic space entered through standard builder gaps — unsealed roof returns, open conduit chases, vent stacks without screens. The neighborhood's first-year pattern is so consistent that we recommend a gap seal at closing for every new Marion Oaks home. Trap the pioneers, seal the pattern, and the house drops off the rats' map.

faqs.q: When can bats be excluded from a McIntosh home?
faqs.a: Bat exclusion is legal in Florida from August 15 through April 15. Excluding or blocking bats during maternity season, April 16 through August 14, is illegal under FWC Rule 68A-9.010. The house bats here are Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats. In maternity season our crew can inspect, identify the roost, and schedule the exclusion for the legal window — and a bat found in a room with a sleeping person is a county health department call first.

McIntosh.wildlife_intro:
In McIntosh, our crew's steady calls are raccoons in attics and chimneys, eastern gray squirrels at soffits and gable vents, and roof rats moving from palms and fruit trees onto rooflines. Opossums and striped skunks work yards after dark, armadillos dig lawns and beds, eastern moles tunnel the sandy ground, and Brazilian free-tailed and evening bats roost in older rooflines through the warm months. The county's habitat — horse farms, Ocala suburbs, forest communities, and spring and river towns — and features such as Ocala National Forest, Silver Springs, Rainbow Springs, Ocklawaha River keep that pressure close to housing in every season.

Florida has no winter shutdown for this work, so McIntosh jobs run year-round, with the one hard legal gate being bats: exclusion is legal only from August 15 through April 15, and maternity-season bat calls become inspection and scheduling. Our crew works under FWC Rule 68A-9.010 with the property owner's authorization — Florida issues no nuisance-trapper license — checks any live trap at least every 24 hours, and seals the entry as part of the job so the next animal cannot use the same opening. Call us at (844) 544-3498 and tell us what you are hearing or seeing.
